articles.summary: Researchers recently investigated the pathways connecting caffeine use disorder, depression, and sleep quality. Their findings illustrate how problematic caffeine consumption and specific use motives correlate with impaired sleep and mental health outcomes.

articles.title: Women diagnosed with ADHD later in life are learning to view hyperfocus as a superpower
articles.summary: A midlife ADHD diagnosis can be life-changing. New research explores how receiving a late diagnosis helps women replace decades of self-blame with self-compassion, allowing them to finally make sense of their hidden emotional struggles.

articles.title: Hidden “immune organ” in the skull may help fight brain cancer
articles.summary: Scientists discovered a hidden “immune organ” inside the skull that acts as a rapid first responder against brain cancer in mice. Strengthening this local immune defense improved tumor rejection and survival, raising the possibility of new treatments that target the skull directly.

articles.title: Higher testosterone linked to opposite suicide risks for older men and women
articles.summary: Testosterone levels may play opposite roles in how older men and women experience suicide risk during severe depression. A new study finds that higher testosterone protects older men, but is linked to increased risk for older women.

articles.title: Long-term study links childhood screen time to slightly better cognitive skills in teenagers
articles.summary: Does screen time always harm developing brains? A new long-term study suggests otherwise, finding that higher childhood screen time and less unsupervised physical activity are actually associated with slightly better cognitive performance in adolescence.

articles.title: Couples bonding over bad habits may age faster at the cellular level
articles.summary: A happy marriage usually promotes a longer life, but a new study shows this benefit depends heavily on shared habits. When partners bond over poor diets and bad sleep, their relationship satisfaction might actually accelerate their biological aging.

articles.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

articles.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
articles.summary: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.

articles.title: Is the phrase “master bedroom” actually harmful? A new psychology study says no
articles.summary: Many universities and businesses now use language guides to eliminate supposedly harmful words like "master bedroom." However, a new study finds these bans may be misguided, as exposure to such terms causes no actual psychological distress.

articles.title: Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
articles.summary: Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating.

articles.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.

articles.summary: A new genetic study reveals that activating the GLP-1 receptor—the target of popular weight-loss drugs—is associated with a lower risk of depression and bipolar disorder, suggesting profound psychiatric benefits beyond shedding pounds.
